raw_text:
Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is an established non-pharmacological strategy to reduce thromboembolism in selected patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation (AF). Its biological rationale is strong: the left atrial appendage (LAA) is the dominant site of thrombus formation in AF, and surgical experience suggested that appendage exclusion might reduce embolic risk [1]. AF itself confers a substantial independent risk of stroke [2], which is refined clinically using scores such as CHADS2 and CHA2DS2-VASc [3], [4], while bleeding risk is commonly estimated with HAS-BLED [5]. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) have improved the therapeutic landscape compared with warfarin [6], [7], [8], [9], but bleeding, frailty, renal dysfunction, drug interactions, and patient preference leave an important niche for LAAC.

The LAA is anatomically variable, and morphology, ostial dimensions, trabeculation, and depth influence both thromboembolic risk and device selection [10]. Surgical occlusion has also regained prominence after LAAOS III, which showed that LAA occlusion during cardiac surgery reduced ischemic stroke or systemic embolism when added to anticoagulation [11]. Percutaneous LAAC, however, is intended for patients in whom long-term oral anticoagulation is unsuitable or undesirable. The procedure generally involves femoral venous access, transseptal puncture, systemic anticoagulation, angiographic and echocardiographic guidance, device deployment, stability testing, and confirmation of an acceptable peri-device leak. Transesophageal echocardiography remains standard, although intracardiac echocardiography and preprocedural cardiac CT are increasingly used.

Early feasibility was demonstrated with the PLAATO system [12], but the randomized evidence base was built around the Watchman device. In PROTECT AF, Watchman LAAC was non-inferior to warfarin for a composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death, although early procedural complications were notable [13]. Subsequent analyses showed a learning-curve effect and improved procedural safety in continued-access experience [14]. Residual peri-device leak was common but usually small; its clinical implications remain nuanced and appear related to leak size, imaging timing, and antithrombotic regimen [15]. Longer-term PROTECT AF follow-up suggested reductions in hemorrhagic stroke and mortality compared with warfarin [16].

Patients unable to take warfarin were not the primary population in the pivotal trials, yet this is a frequent real-world indication. The ASAP study supported Watchman implantation followed by antiplatelet therapy in patients with contraindications to oral anticoagulation [17]. PREVAIL, designed partly to confirm safety and efficacy with more experienced operators, met safety targets but had mixed efficacy endpoints because of low event rates [18]. Pooled and longer-term randomized data reinforced the concept that LAAC trades an upfront procedural risk for durable protection with less hemorrhagic stroke than warfarin [19], [20]. Large registries such as EWOLUTION further showed high implant success and acceptable 1-year outcomes in older, comorbid populations, many of whom did not receive warfarin after implantation [21].

Alternative device platforms broadened practice. The Amplatzer Cardiac Plug and later Amulet use a lobe-and-disc design that may be advantageous in certain anatomies [22], [23]. Multicenter experience with the Cardiac Plug demonstrated feasibility but also highlighted device-related thrombus and procedural complications [24]. The prospective global Amulet registry reported high closure rates and low residual leak at follow-up [25]. In the randomized Amulet IDE trial, Amulet was non-inferior to Watchman for safety and effectiveness and achieved superior anatomic closure, although procedural complications differed between devices [26]. The next-generation Watchman FLX was designed to improve conformability, recapturability, and sealing; PINNACLE FLX reported high implant success and low major adverse event rates [27].

Important complications include pericardial effusion, device embolization, procedure-related stroke, vascular injury, peri-device leak, and device-related thrombus (DRT). DRT occurs in a minority of patients but is clinically important because it is associated with embolic events and usually prompts temporary anticoagulation when feasible [28]. Antithrombotic therapy after LAAC remains individualized. Original Watchman protocols used warfarin plus aspirin followed by dual antiplatelet therapy and then aspirin; contemporary practice includes DOAC-based, dual-antiplatelet, or single-antiplatelet strategies depending on bleeding and thrombotic risk. Observational data support DOAC use as an alternative to warfarin in the early post-implant period [29], but the optimal regimen for patients with extreme bleeding risk remains uncertain.

LAAC should not be viewed as a universal substitute for anticoagulation. DOACs remain first-line for most eligible patients with AF. The strongest indication for percutaneous LAAC is a patient with high thromboembolic risk and an unacceptable long-term anticoagulation burden—particularly prior major bleeding, recurrent bleeding despite correction of reversible causes, or inability to maintain safe anticoagulation. PRAGUE-17 extended comparative evidence to high-risk patients treated with DOACs, showing LAAC was non-inferior to DOAC therapy for a composite of thromboembolic, bleeding, and cardiovascular outcomes [30]. Future priorities include defining optimal post-implant pharmacotherapy, improving imaging thresholds for leaks and DRT, clarifying outcomes in chronic kidney disease and prior intracranial hemorrhage, and integrating LAAC into shared decision-making rather than using it as a device-driven intervention.
